projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Marvin Fishman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Today is November 11, 2015. I am the interviewer, Arthur D. Kessler, and this morning I am speaking with Marvin Fishman. His birth date is [birth date redacted]. He is a veteran of the U.S. Army and was in this service from 1943 to 1945. The beginning time of the interview is 10:11 a.m. I want get a little bit about your background, your childhood, your parents. I'd like to find out what you were doing on December 7th when you learned that Pearl Harbor was attacked, you know.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Well, in '43 I was only 17. I made sergeant in two weeks, and they sent me to Germany. I was only 17 years old. To sergeant.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: We'll get to that, okay? I have to do this formality, and we'll start, all right?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Whenever you want to ask questions, don't hesitate. I'll help you.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Okay. Today is November 11th, 2015. I am the interviewer, Arthur D. Kessler, and this morning I'm speaking Marvin Fishman. His date of birth is January 6th, 1926. He's a veteran of the U.S. Army and was in the service from 1943 to 1945. The beginning time of this interview is --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Instead of sending me back to Illinois, when the war ended, they sent me to Fort Dix, New Jersey, to go to captain school to be a captain. But I wasn't 21 yet, so they gave me a three-week pass to come back home and give the paperwork to my mother and father to sign it if they wanted me to go to captain school. But when I got home, they said no.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So it's 10:10a.m., and we're going to start. Mr. Fishman, it's an honor to talk to you this morning. And my first question is, I'd like to know about your family, your background, where you were born, and a little bit about your parents.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I was born in Illinois in 1926, January the 6th, 1926. I have one child, one daughter; lives in Wrigleyville.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And your parents?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: They're all dead, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And do you have any siblings?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I have one brother left. He's eight years younger than I am.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, in nineteen -- where did you go to high school?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Ballard -- I forget the name of it. I used to walk from 15th and Lawndale all the way there, every day; and coming back, walking all the way back.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So you grew up on the south side of Chicago?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: On the south side, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall December 7th, 1941, when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, putting the United States into World War II?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember what you were doing on that day?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I was still in school at that time.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And how old were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: 15, I think.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And you entered the service?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah. They put me right into Germany. I was only 17 years old.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you sign up, or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Drafted.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And when you were drafted, how old were you?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: 17. Where did you do your basic training?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I don't recall, but I made sergeant in two weeks. I got it right here, sergeant.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And what type of unit were you placed in?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Army.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Okay. That's in the army. Were you in the infantry?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And when did you land in Europe? Do you recall?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were in Europe in 1943?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: When were you on the Mainland in --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Right there.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: '3, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Were you in Italy?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, Germany.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And when you -- well, let's flow with it. Do you recall how you got from -- were you first in England?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You went straight from the United States to --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Into Germany.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Into the mainland?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall how you got from the United States over to Europe?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: They took me on a boat.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall the boat?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't recall, no.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall what port you landed in?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you go directly into Germany?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall the time of the year?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: That's the year. Do you recall whether it was summer, winter, fall?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: But, see, when the war ended in '45, instead of sending me back to Illinois, they sent me to Fort Dix, New Jersey, because they knew what type of person I was. I'm a friendly person. I help everybody I can. They sent me there to go to officer school to be captain, but I wasn't 21 yet. Because you can't be a -- you can't go to school unless you're 21 years old. So they gave me a three-week pass to go back home and give the paperwork to my mother and father and see if they would okay it or not, but they said no. Because I was fighting every day in Germany.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: They were with me with machine guns, shooting at us all the day long because we liberated three concentration camps with Jewish people in there. And we put them on the boat so they cold go wherever they want to go.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall the name of the concentrations camps that you --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: One name was Auschwitz.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were in Auschwitz?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall the men that were in your particular unit?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: What type of weapon did you carry? Do you recall?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Just handguns.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you carry an M1 rifle?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No rifle.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You had no rifle?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: They never gave me a rifle.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You just had pistols?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: We had pistols, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: And my cemetery was Shalom Park.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Where they got buried, everybody I knew, it was at Shalom Park.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: It's way out -- way out west, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Here?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: On Rand Road.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Who's buried in Shalom Park?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Right now, my mother -- my mother, my father, and now -- and my wife. When my wife died -- she died at 93 years old. We were married 66 years. And we only had one child in Wrigleyville. But she's very good to us now. She does whatever we want to do and bring our apartment anything we need. I give her the money to pay for it, because I'm in the market, very heavy in the stock market. Very heavy since 1947.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, when you were in Europe, do you know any of the specific areas that you were in?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't remember. Near the water, I know. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, on your form, you said that you were in the Black Forest campaign.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, yeah, Black Forest, almost to the time, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah. I remember that, and 17 of my boys got killed, because they never showed us what a land mine looked like. As soon as they touched it, boom, they exploded and killed them right away. 17 out of 27.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So your unit suffered heavy casualties?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, very heavy casualties. And me too. They found I'm 110 percent disabled.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall where you were --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: -- on the day --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't recall.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: -- that you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you spend time in a hospital?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: How long were you in the hospital?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I was there for at least a couple months, I think. Yeah, they got all the records and everything else.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And you had indicated to me earlier when we were talking that you were in the Third Army; you were in Patton's army?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Third Army, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember anything specific about the combat that you were in?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: We were fighting every day, because they didn't want to us let the people go out of the concentration camps. And I put them on the boat. But I paid the sailor. I gave him the money to do it. He took the people, put them into the cabins. So he didn't tell the captain about it. And he was told just to take the people wherever they want to go now.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember -- do you know where the boat took these people?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember the names of any individuals that were in your platoon?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, no. I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember who your commanding officer was, or your platoon leader?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I think his name was Raton, or Patton, or something like that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: When -- do you recall the day that you learned that the war was over?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Well, they sent us the information.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: In 1945, and I was only 19 years old.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember where you were when you got the word that the war was over?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: In Germany.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Any --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: -- particular area or town?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: And they sent me to Fort Dix, New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Was this when the war was over?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Was this when the war was over?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: '45, the war was over.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And that's when you were sent to Fort Dix?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Fort Dix, New Jersey, to be a captain, because they knew what type of character I was. I'm just a friendship person. That's all I want from people. If you help people, you might well go in the ground. That's the way I looked at life all the time.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you -- how long were you at Fort Dix, New Jersey?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, maybe about a couple weeks.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And then after Fort Dix, New Jersey?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: In Fort Dix, New Jersey, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And after you were there --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: And then they sent me back home. They gave me a three-week pass to go back home with a round trip airfare to ask my parents if they would okay me going to school because I wasn't 21 yet.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And after you came home, you talked to your parents?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: They said no.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And when your three-week pass was up, what did you do then?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I didn't do nothing. I went out of the army.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you get mustered out here in Illinois, or did you have to go back to Fort Dix?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were here?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: After you mustered out of the army, what did you do then?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I worked for McDonald's for six years as cashier, and then I went into the currency exchange business, and I helped them people. I interviewed -- I saved them a lot of money because I bought all kinds of things for them so they would have money at the end of the year.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you live in an assisted living facility?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Where do you live?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Where do I live? In Skokie.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you have your own apartment?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Let's get back on task here. I guess the best way to proceed on this is for you to just have, like, an open mic to talk about anything that you really --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Anything you want to know, I'll help you.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Anything that you remember about your experience when you were --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Were fighting?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: When you were fighting in the army.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, in the Black Forest, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So if you just want to tell us about what your experiences were as much you can remember.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: What they tried to do, they tried to have us away from the camp so we shouldn't let the people get out of the concentration camps. And they kept fighting with us all the time, and we kept fighting with them because we wanted to save the people.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, did you come into any close contact with German soldiers?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They came with us with machine guns, and they kept shooting at us all the time, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And do you remember what specific -- your first actual combat encounter was? Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: It was about, I would say, in the end of '43, yeah. The beginning of '43, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember anything specific about that encounter?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, did you -- so you were an infantryman, right?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were an infantryman?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So you did a lot of walking?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember any particular areas of Germany that you were in --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: -- and where you walked --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. We weren't that far from the Black Forest, I know. 17 of my boys got killed, because they never showed us what a land mine looked like. Soon as they touched the land mine, exploded and killed them right away. I went through a lot of hell over there. But like I say, I'm here to help as many people as I can. I don't care who you are. If you need some help, you call Marvin, and Marvin's going to be here to help you. That's the way I've always been all my life.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: When you were in Europe, did you used to write letters home?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You didn't write letters home? Did you get letters from your parents?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Sometimes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you -- were you on the line constantly? Did you get any leave time, any passes to come off the front lines?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So you were in constant combat?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Combat all the time, yeah. Yeah. And last week, I noticed my throat was all sore. I couldn't talk at all. But then I put Listerine in there, and I put some towels around my neck, and it helped me a little bit so I can talk a little bit to you. Because you're a very important person to talk to.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Oh, thank you.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Anytime I can help you in any way, don't hesitate. I don't want nothing for it, just friendship. That's all.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: I appreciate that, Mr. Fishman.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: You see, I'm what you call a professional dancer. I love to dance, and when I volunteered at the different places, I got ten to 15 women lined up with hugs and kisses and smiles just to dance with Marvin all week long, all afternoon. And I enjoyed that, and they enjoyed it. And, no, there's nothing else involved, no sex or nothing. And in January, I'll be 90 years old. And you'd be surprised. When my daughter called me last week, she said, dad, I got cards and cards from Florida and from California. They want to come for your birthday party, all that way, coming here. So they're going to come, the birthday party's January 10th, and they're going to come from California and Florida. I have 26 people coming to the birthday party. It's going to cost me over $600 -- $616,000 [SIC] it's going to cost to feed them for dinner that day.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Okay, Mr. Fishman, back to your experiences in Europe. Were you ever in Italy?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You never were in Italy?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Or Cicely?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Or France?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: In France I was, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, when I got wounded in France. They sent me to France for rehabilitation.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were wounded in France?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I got wounded in Germany.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember where in France the military hospital was?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: The military -- it was right in the -- right on Champs-Elysées.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were in Paris?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: In Paris, yeah. That's where I met my first girl. I never had sex with anybody until I met her. Ha-ha-ha-ha-ha.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: I thought you were wounded.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I got out of the hospital. They sent me to Fort -- over there for rehabilitation. So that's where I went.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So how long were you in France rehabilitating?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Couple, three weeks I think it was.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall -- you received two purple hearts. The first purple heart that you received, do you remember where on your body you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, my hands. My hands and my knees. They took everything out of my knees and my elbows and everything else, and they found I'm 110 percent disabled.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Was that wound, was that from shrapnel?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And so you were in the hospital recuperating?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And then you got sent back to the front line?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Were you put back in the same unit?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Same unit, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall the second time you were wounded, what happened there?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't remember. But when we went to Washington, we went to Washington three, four -- three months ago, and we had a very good time there. They treated us very, very well, the veterans.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you go on an honor flight?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, an honor flight. You got it right here, honor flight, right here. Right there. Honor flight. Yeah. I got this, and I got my name on there, and my sergeant.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you -- did they take you to the World War II memorial?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yes, they did.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: What did you think of the memorial?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: It was wonderful. So many people were involved, and so many people got killed in there, in the war. But thank God we were able to live a little bit. Because when I told them that I was 110 percent, they said when you're 100 percent, you should be dead. But I managed to live. Ha-ha. And when I went to see my Dr. Lazar, he said, Marvin, you got 18 more months to go.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: When did he say that?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, some time ago.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: More than 18 months.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah. See, when my wife died, she was 93. And so when she died, I went to the doctor, and I said, "My wife died." She said, "What do you mean, she died? I saw her just six days ago, and I told her she'd have another ten years to go." I said you never know what's going to happen the next day. You don't know that. You can walk around the corner and get a heart attack. You don't know what's going to happen. But thank God, she was a wonderful woman, and married 66 years, which is a record, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, after Germany surrendered in 1945, were you part of the occupation force in Germany?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. Sent me right to Fort Dix, New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You got sent right home, huh?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And you were 19?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: 19. That's -- '45, yeah. January the 6th, 1926.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, did you -- do you have photographs --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: -- that were taken when you were in the army?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I don't think -- I think they took photographs, but I never got the pictures. That's why they take my pictures all the time now. But I was glad I was able to serve the right way. Because if I can help anybody, I'll be there to help. I don't care who you are, red, yellow, green or blue. If you're hurt on the floor, Marvin's going to be there to help you. One good thing, I found a new woman at Brookdale. Yeah. I found her. And she's younger than I am, but she's a nice woman, and we're just looking for friendship. That's all, baby.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Let's get back to the army, okay?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Let's get back to the army.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember anything about the army food?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Third Army.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You were in the Third Army?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: What about the food?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: The food?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Yeah. What was that like?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: It was fair.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you eat a lot of C-rations?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: How often did you -- let's talk about the weather. Was it cold in Germany?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you remember the specific dates that you were actually in Germany?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. I know it was '43, I know. That's all I remember. And the war was over in '45, and that's where they sent me out, right away, to Fort Dix. Because they knew what type of a person I was, and I can help everybody I can, and they knew that. So that's why they sent me there. Because you got to be 21 in order to go back in the school. You know that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you recall your basic training?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, I don't recall where it was. But I know they made me sergeant right away. It's on my record how I made sergeant right away. I got two purple hearts in the war, and that's why they sent me that letter in 2006. The wounds I got, I'm 110 percent disabled. But thank God I'm able to do everything I want to do by myself. I don't need no help, except to put on the -- they put on my stockings every morning at 7:00 o'clock, yeah, with the cream, yeah. Because then my legs won't get swelled. But my daughter was very pleased the way it turned out. Legs got down, and everything was working okay.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, how did you learn about this Veteran's project?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: About the what?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: About the Veteran's project to be interviewed today.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I got a letter in the mail. I got to be downstairs in Brookdale at 7:00 o'clock, and they pick you up at 7:15, and they take you out here, yeah. It wasn't that far to go. I think it was 30 miles, I think. Did you think that was 30 miles? Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Is Brookdale in Niles?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Brookdale in Niles, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: It's about 30 miles.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, I was in a one-bedroom apartment. And you'd be surprised, my friend. When they found out I am a World War II veteran, they took off $500 off the rent to show that they appreciate what I did. I thought this was very nice of them to do that. But the way they charge, they charge you so much money for doing anything for you. That's how they make their money, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you belong to any veteran's organizations today?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. They want you to join it, and they want you to give them $50 to get in there.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, when you were in the army, did you develop any close friendships with any other soldiers?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Not that much, no. No. I was the leader, and they followed -- whatever I told them to do, they did, yeah. Because I'm an experienced man about that, so I know what to do, and so I do it all by myself. I didn't need no help. No help. Everybody has caregivers, you know, and they come with you and everything else. I don't have that. I do it all by myself.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, in addition to the purple hearts that you received, did you receive any other awards?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you get a combat award?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah. They gave me that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: How did you make sergeant so quickly? Do you know?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: They knew my character.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: You had leadership capabilities?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah. The same when I met my wife. I had my younger brother's bar mitzvah. I was sitting in the back room, and a woman come up to me, said, Marvin, there's a woman up front. She wants to meet you. I said, who am I supposed to meet so important she wants to meet me? She likes your character. So I went with her up front, and three months, we fell in love with each other and got married right away, in 1948, June the 20th, yeah. And we had one daughter. My wife only wanted one child. We had one daughter. And then when my daughter got married, I went to the Federal Reserve Bank, and I bought a $500 bill. At that time, they were making them. And I put the bill in an envelope to my first child's child, and 50 years later, she came up to me, she says, dad, I'm not going to have any children. I don't want to go through what mother went through. We lost two children before she was born, and my wife had to be in bed for six to eight months. So I had to take that bill over on Touhy and Milwaukee. There was an office there, and they bought bills and coins and things like that. They gave me $590 for that bill. And a month later, the man that gave me the money called me on than the phone. He says, Marvin, if you waited another month, I could give you a thousand dollars.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Is there anything additional that you would like to add about your experience in World War II?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Well, I went through a lot of hell, but thank God I was there to do it. And I did it, and I didn't complain about nothing. I don't complain about nothing. Because if I don't like the menu, I just order chicken or fish. They always have that. And they were very good on the soup. But they put too much salt in the soup. So I couldn't have the soup until I get clearance from my doctor. And when I went to take the blood pressure two weeks ago, it started off at 220. Now, that's very high. But ten minutes later, after I sat around and I breathe deeply, it went down to 140. So that's what the blood pressure is now. And my cholesterol is down to. And now they send us back to Brookdale now?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Not yet. I have a few more questions. Now, you talked about the people that were liberated from the concentration camps --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: -- that you helped get aboard a boat.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you speak to any of these people?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Were you able to speak to any of these people?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I just asked them where they wanted to go. And I told that to the sailor, and I gave him the money for it too, out of my own pocket. Nobody else paid for them but me. I gave him $500 for three boats.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Who did you give the $500 to?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: The sailors.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Were they U.S. sailors? Was this an American boat?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, U.S. sailors, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Do you know where these people were being taken?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. I don't remember where, but they got the boat -- they put them on the boat, and that's why the Germans were so much against us. They didn't want to us to do that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: How were you able to communicate with these --

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: These people that you eliminated from the concentration camps, how were you able to communicate with them? Do you speak German?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I speak a little German, yeah. And I speak a little Jewish. Jewish people, all of them.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: So you spoke Yiddish?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: And you were able to communicate with them through speaking Yiddish?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Yeah, danken got far vos. You know what that is?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: No. I know a few words. I don't really speak Yiddish. What did you say?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Danken got far vos.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Thank God for that. As long as I was able to help people, it made my happy about it. And they come into me with, I told you, hugs and kisses and smiles. And that's all I want. And I was dancing with them all afternoon in the summertime, because we had four or five schools around the area that came to play music every afternoon. And that's what I did. I taught them how to dance, and I danced with them. And they were very happy, and I was happy about it. If they smile, it makes me smile too. You'd be surprised all the people come up to me for advice about investigating money and everything, because I'm in the market since 1947.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Back to the sailors that you gave money to.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Huh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Why did you have to pay these sailors money?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Well, they wanted to get paid for what they were going to do.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: The American sailors did?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: The sailors, yes. Yeah. And they took the people right off, and they put them right in the cabin. I was very happy to do that. I had the money to do it, so I didn't complain about nobody. I didn't tell anthing to anybody else, just to you.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: How many people were there?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I don't remember the numbers. There were a lot of people, men and women. And a few children too, yeah. But that was over 70 years ago, and it's hard to remember things like that so many years ago. You know that. But I tell everybody that I meet, if they need any help, don't hesitate to knock on my door or call me on the phone, and I'll come down and help you. They say you want to get paid? I said, no. I'll help you whatever you want me to help you with.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, was this only one time that you had to help these people get aboard a boat?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: I didn't see them do it, because I gave the people to the sailor, and he did it, and I went back to my place, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: What place was that?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: In Germany. Yeah. But you'd be surprised. When we went to Washington for the honor flight, over 200 people came up to us with their hands out and thanked us for our service to our country. Over 217 people came up to us with their hands out and thanked us for what we did. And what is your first name again?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Arthur.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Arthur, okay. Yeah. See, a couple weeks ago, I can't talk like this. My throat was all -- hurting all the time. So I put Listerine. I rinsed my mouth out with Listerine, and I put towels around my neck so I can talk a little bit better.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Now, you said you had made sergeant in two weeks after you were in the army.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Right here. Right there. And there is the -- I got from them too.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you get any kind of recognition when you were in the field?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: When you were in the field, when you were in combat situations.

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. But the Germans came up to us with machine guns and a lot of fighting all the time. But they were fighting the Russians too, you know, at that time.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Oh, when the war was over and you were in Germany, did you come into contact with any Russians?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No, no. They sent us right away to Fort Dix, New Jersey, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: Did you have any contact with any free French or the British?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. I was all by myself at that time.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: I don't have anything else. Do you have anything else that you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Marvin Fishman
sp.p: No. But you did a very good job, Arthur. Thank you very much for your help.

sp.speaker: Arthur Kessler
sp.p: It's a pleasure, Mr. Fishman. Okay. I guess we'll conclude the interview. This interview is being concluded at 10:52 a.m.
